Surrogacy (Ethics)
SUR-uh-guh-see
noun (Christian bioethics)
The practice by which a woman bears a child for another couple or individual, whether using the surrogate's own egg (traditional surrogacy) or an embryo created from others' gametes (gestational surrogacy). Christian bioethics engages substantive concerns: the commodification of childbearing, the introduction of a third party into procreation, and the separation of motherhood into genetic, gestational, and social components.

Biblical Definition

The practice by which a woman bears a child for another couple or individual. Distinguished into (1) traditional surrogacy (the surrogate's own egg is used, making her the genetic and gestational mother); (2) gestational surrogacy (an embryo created from others' gametes is implanted, making the surrogate the gestational but not genetic mother). Christian bioethics engages surrogacy with substantive concern. The principal ethical concerns: (1) The commodification of childbearing: commercial surrogacy treats the womb as a rentable service and the child as a contracted product, contrary to the biblical dignity of childbearing and the child. (2) The introduction of a third party into procreation: surrogacy introduces a woman other than the wife into the procreative process, contrary to the one-flesh exclusivity of marriage. (3) The fragmentation of motherhood: surrogacy splits motherhood into genetic (egg donor), gestational (surrogate), and social (intended mother) components, contrary to the biblical integration of these in the one mother. (4) The bonding and relinquishment problem: the gestational bond between the surrogate and the child she carries is severed at birth by contract, contrary to the substantive biblical understanding of the maternal-child bond formed in the womb (Psalm 22:9-10; Isaiah 49:15). The biblical narrative of Sarah and Hagar (Genesis 16) is the cautionary OT precedent: Sarah's attempt to obtain a child through her servant Hagar produced grievous family conflict and was not the LORD's appointed means. The patriarchal-Reformed reader engages surrogacy with substantive caution: the commercial commodification of childbearing, the introduction of third parties into procreation, and the fragmentation of motherhood are substantive concerns; the genuine grief of infertility is real but does not justify the substantive ethical problems of surrogacy; adoption (the substantive biblical pattern of receiving children not biologically one's own into the covenant household) is the substantive alternative.

Webster 1828 Definition

The practice by which a woman bears a child for another; Christian bioethics engages the commodification of childbearing, the introduction of a third party into procreation, the fragmentation of motherhood, and the bonding-relinquishment problem; Sarah and Hagar (Genesis 16) the cautionary OT precedent.

SURROGACY (ETHICS), n. (Christian bioethics) A woman bears a child for another couple or individual. Traditional surrogacy (surrogate's own egg) or gestational surrogacy (others' gametes implanted). Concerns: (1) commodification of childbearing (commercial surrogacy treats womb as rentable service, child as contracted product); (2) introduction of a third party into procreation (contrary to marital one-flesh exclusivity); (3) fragmentation of motherhood (genetic/gestational/social split); (4) bonding-relinquishment problem (severing the womb-formed maternal-child bond by contract, Psalm 22:9-10; Isaiah 49:15). Sarah and Hagar (Genesis 16) the cautionary OT precedent. Adoption the substantive biblical alternative.

Key Scripture

Genesis 16:1-2 — "Now Sarai Abram's wife bare him no children: and she had an handmaid, an Egyptian, whose name was Hagar. And Sarai said unto Abram, Behold now, the LORD hath restrained me from bearing: I pray thee, go in unto my maid; it may be that I may obtain children by her."

Psalm 22:9-10 — "But thou art he that took me out of the womb: thou didst make me hope when I was upon my mother's breasts. I was cast upon thee from the womb: thou art my God from my mother's belly."

Isaiah 49:15 — "Can a woman forget her sucking child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee."

Genesis 1:28 — "And God blessed them, and God said unto them, Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth."

Modern Corruption

Surrogacy commodifies childbearing, introduces a third party into procreation, fragments motherhood, and severs the womb-formed maternal-child bond by contract; Sarah and Hagar (Genesis 16) is the cautionary OT precedent.

expand to see more

The substantive ethical concerns with surrogacy are multiple. Commercial surrogacy commodifies childbearing, treating the womb as a rentable service and the child as a contracted product, contrary to the biblical dignity of childbearing and the inestimable worth of the child as an image-bearer. Surrogacy introduces a woman other than the wife into the procreative process, contrary to the one-flesh exclusivity of marriage (Genesis 2:24). Surrogacy fragments motherhood into genetic, gestational, and social components, contrary to the biblical integration of these in the one mother. And surrogacy severs the gestational bond between the surrogate and the child she carries by contract at birth, contrary to the substantive biblical understanding of the maternal-child bond formed in the womb (Psalm 22:9-10; Isaiah 49:15). The biblical narrative of Sarah and Hagar (Genesis 16) is the cautionary OT precedent: Sarah's attempt to obtain a child through her servant Hagar — an ancient-Near-Eastern surrogacy arrangement — produced grievous family conflict (Hagar's contempt, Sarah's harshness, Ishmael's enmity) and was emphatically not the LORD's appointed means; the LORD gave Sarah her own son Isaac in His own time. The patriarchal-Reformed reader engages surrogacy with substantive caution and commends adoption (the substantive biblical pattern of receiving children into the covenant household) as the substantive alternative for the infertile couple.

Hebrew Roots

A woman bears a child for another; commodification, third-party procreation, fragmented motherhood concerns; Sarah and Hagar (Genesis 16); adoption the alternative.
